evidence: About 25,000 gens de couleur libres beside about 30,000 white colonists; an elite owned plantations and enslaved people. A long history of discriminatory law. M1 = 0 is unverified: no source here shows commissions in colonial service.
sources: 1789 election in Saint-Domingue <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1789_French_legislative_election_in_Saint-Domingue>; Petition of December 2, 1789 <https://colonyincrisis.lib.umd.edu/1789/12/02/request-and-petition-from-the-citizens-of-color-of-the-french-isles-and-colonies-december-2-1789/>

evidence: Ogé’s revolt for equal rights; the colonial order puts it down.
The colonial authorities execute Ogé and Chavannes.
The National Assembly grants rights to free men of color born of free parents (May 15); the colonists refuse to apply it.
The Assembly revokes the May decree (September 24); gens de couleur libres in the West take up arms on their own.
The April 4, 1792 decree gives full equal rights; commissions open (Rigaud becomes a general in the South).
Rigaud holds the South for the Republic; equality is in force.
War of the South: Toussaint, governor for France, defeats Rigaud, who goes into exile; Dessalines leads reprisals against Rigaud’s supporters (scale disputed).
General amnesty (July 1800); some officers of color serve under Toussaint.
Officers of color land with Leclerc (Pétion, Rigaud). The 1792 equality law is in force. Napoleon’s secret instructions (October 31, 1801) plan deportation of leaders, but they are not public.
Toussaint submits; officers of color still command. The law of May 20, 1802 keeps slavery in the colonies that never applied abolition.

In Guadeloupe, Richepanse restores slavery and reserves the title of citizen for whites (July 16–17), repealing the 1792 equality law there. A July 2 decree bars people of color from entering France. Disarmament breeds the “greatest discontent.”
sources: Richepanse <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Richepanse>; Decree of 29 March 1815 (history of the 1802 decrees) <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decree_of_29_March_1815>

evidence: Pétion and Clervaux leave French service (October 13–14). Leclerc disarms about 1,200 native soldiers; Black and mulatto prisoners are drowned at Le Cap. Leclerc’s orders call for deporting leading officers of color.
sources: Haiti: Her History and Her Detractors, ch. IX <https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Haiti:_Her_History_and_Her_Detractors/Part_I:_Chapter_IX>; French Navy and the expedition <https://ijnh.seahistory.org/the-ugly-duckling-the-french-navy-and-the-saint-domingue-expedition1801-1803/>

evidence: Petits blancs (shopkeepers, artisans, laborers) sit below the grands blancs. Whites alone hold full rights; slavery is in force. P1 = 0.5 is a judgment: a modest material stake.
The northern uprising destroys plantations; whites’ persons and property are at risk.
Equal rights for free people of color end the racial privilege over them.
Battle of Cap-Français: settlers fight the commissioners; the city burns and thousands flee.
Sonthonax frees the enslaved in the North; the Convention abolishes slavery.
Toussaint governs; slavery stays abolished; white planters are invited back to reclaim property; whites live under a Black-led government.
Leclerc restores French command; the secret instructions plan a return to the old order.
Guadeloupe: slavery restored and citizenship reserved for whites.
War resumes; French forces lose ground.
Vertières: the French army is defeated and leaves.
Marronage; the Code Noir forbids the enslaved to carry arms.
Northern uprising (August 22, 1791): one province, irregular arms.
Biassou and Jean-François ally with Spain; the commissioners free Black men who fight for them.
Toussaint brings his army to the French side.
Toussaint’s forces secure the British withdrawal.
Toussaint governs the whole island; the 1801 constitution binds cultivators to plantation labor. Army size not found in these sources.
Toussaint’s army fights Leclerc’s 31,131 troops.
Toussaint submits; the disarmament campaign begins.
General insurrection after the October defections.
Unified command at Arcahaie; Polish legionnaires defect with artillery skills; the French force collapses (manuscript :3665, :14111).
Vertières (November 18, 1803).
